sourceBindings.text: Use the beach-sand analogy carefully
A student says: 'All desert soils are hot, pure sand, contain under 1% organic matter and are salty.'
The analogy only starts a question about water and nutrient retention.
Aridisol classification depends on moisture regime and profile features; cold Aridisols exist.
Texture, organic matter and salts must be measured for the site.
Reject the universal claim; propose a texture/profile/OM/EC investigation.

sourceBindings.text: Read the pilot-plot report
The 10 m × 10 m sandy-loam plot reports organic matter 0.8%, EC 3.5 dS/m and 'slightly saline' borewell water with no methods attached.
The area is 100 m²; 0.8% OM is a measured site value.
Request soil EC preparation, sampling depth/date and the borewell ECw plus ions.
Only if the soil value is verified as ECe at 25°C can an ECe-specific 2–4 dS/m interpretation be used; crop sensitivity still varies.
Mark salinity class and crop choice provisional; preserve all numbers and units without guessing the method.

sourceBindings.text: Water can be present but difficult to use
A root-zone sample is moist, yet a crop looks stressed and a reliable soil test confirms elevated salts.
Physical drought is less likely if water is truly available, but salt-induced osmotic stress remains plausible.
Check the specific ion pattern for possible Na/Ca/K imbalance or chloride injury separately.
Analyse irrigation water and drainage before adding more water or attempting leaching.
Distinguish osmotic uptake difficulty from an empty reservoir and from direct ion toxicity.

sourceBindings.text: What does a hard layer prove?
A spade stops at a hard layer below a dryland plot.
A carbonate-cemented caliche layer is one possible cause and can impede roots or drainage.
Compaction, gypsum-cemented or other horizons may also be hard.
Examine profile and composition before naming or breaking the layer.
Record the obstruction and test its origin; do not label it caliche from resistance alone.
